question.text: For a reaction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math> the half lives are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>100</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>50</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></math> when the concentration of reactant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0</mn><mo> </mo><mi>mol</mi><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>=</mo></math> respectively. The order of the reaction is

solution.text:
The relation between half-life and initial concentration of nth order reaction can be written as follows,

t12∝1A0n-1

100∝10.5n-1

50∝11n-1

21=10.5n-1

21=2n-1

n-1=1

n=2

order =2

For the second order reactions half-life is inversely proportional to initial concentration.
